Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), (Sleeping Sickness)

Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), also known as sleeping sickness, is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei parasites, transmitted by tsetse flies (Glossina species). It occurs in two forms: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (chronic, West and Central Africa) and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (acute, East and Southern Africa). The disease is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and is nearly 100% fatal if untreated.

Symptoms and signs

HAT progresses in two stages: Stage one, No CNS involvement (CSF: ≤5 white blood cells/µL, no trypanosomes) and stage two, CNS involvement (CSF: >5 white blood cells/µL, trypanosomes detected, or elevated protein).

Leishmaniasis

Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease caused by protozoans of the genus Leishmania, transmitted primarily by the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. It presents in three main forms cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral.

runs.text: Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease caused by protozoans of the genus Leishmania, transmitted primarily by the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. It presents in three main forms cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral.

blocks.text: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), also known as kala-azar, is fatal if left untreated in over 95% of cases. It is characterized by irregular bouts of fever, weight loss, enlargement of the spleen and liver, and anaemia. Most cases occur in Brazil, east Africa and India.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is the most common form and causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers, on exposed parts of the body. These can leave life-long scars and cause serious disability or stigma. About 95% of CL cases occur in the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East and central Asia. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL) leads to partial or total destruction of mucous membranes of the nose, mouth and throat. Over 90% of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis cases occur in Bolivia, Brazil, Ethiopia and Peru.

Pharmacological Management

The treatment of leishmaniasis depends on several factors including type of disease, concomitant pathologies, parasite species and geographic location. Leishmaniasis is a treatable and curable disease, which requires an immunocompetent system because medicines will not get rid of the parasite from the body, thus the risk of relapse if immunosuppression occurs. All patients diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis require prompt and complete treatment.

Snake Bites

A snakebite can be life-threatening if the snake is venomous. Less than 10% of 3500 snake species are venomous and they include different species of Cobras, Mambas and Adders which are endemic in Tanzania. Clinical Presentation of a snakebite varies depending on the type of envenomation a snake causes. The severity of the symptoms depends on the amount of venom the snake injects into the victim. Some snakebites (10-30%) can be considered as dry bites where no venom is injected. As a late appearance if symptoms after a snakebite is possible up to 24 hours a close monitoring needs to be conducted in this time frame.

In case of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom administration mild anaphylaxis can occur in around 20-30% of the cases and severe anaphylaxis can occur in around 5-10% of the cases. Venom Ophthalmia

Spitting Cobras, like the Black-necked Spitting Cobra, the Ashe’s Spitting Cobra and the Red Spitting Cobra can spit the venom into the eyes or onto the skin of a patient. Venom on intact skin can just be washed with water. Venom which was spilt into the eyes of a patient can cause severe complications including blindness.

Ensure the venom doesn’t enter the mouth of the victim.
The victim should be instructed to open and close the eyes under water.
Assess the patient under the slit lamp and check for corneal erosions.
Pharmacological Management When Corneal Erosion is Present
Clinical Indication
Management
Prevention of Secondary Infection
A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon into affected eye(s) 3–4 times daily until healed and for an additional 48 hours

blocks.text: OR
A: oxytetracycline 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 2–4 times daily for 5–7 days
OR
A: erythromycin 0.5% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 4 times daily for 3–5 days
Pain and Photophobia
S: homatropine 2% eye drops, 1 drop twice daily for 2–3 days
OR
D: cyclopentolate 1% eye drops, 1 drop twice daily for 2–3 days
Systemic Analgesia
A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN (maximum 4 g/day)
OR
A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours PRN (if no contraindications)
Lubrication
C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.3% 1–2 drops as needed
When No Corneal Erosion is Present
Clinical Indication
Management
Prophylaxis and Symptom Relief
A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 3–4 times daily for 48 hours
OR
A: oxytetracycline 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 2–4 times daily for 48 hours
Pain Relief (if required)
A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN
Lubrication
C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.3% 1–2 drops as needed
Note:
No Polyvalent Snake Antivenom is required for venom ophthalmia.
Venom ophthalmia is a form of envenoming which can present with visual symptoms only and can lead to blindness if left untreated.
Encourage the patient not to rub the eye.
Routine use of topical corticosteroids is not recommended.
Routine eye patching is not recommended.
Patients with persistent pain, visual impairment, corneal ulceration, or non-healing epithelial defects should be referred urgently for ophthalmological assessment.
